eviscerate

ih-VIS-uh-rayt · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To eviscerate is to disembowel, or in a non-literal sense to deprive something of its essential substance or strength.

The butcher quickly eviscerated the fish before packing it in ice.

Example

The new budget cuts eviscerated the department, leaving barely enough staff to answer the phones.

The department wasn't just trimmed -- its essential core was gutted out, leaving almost nothing functional, which is exactly eviscerate used in a non-literal sense.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

gut: To gut something is to strip out its insides or its essential contents — you gut a fish, a burned building, or a bill in committee. It is the plain, everyday twin of eviscerate, which is the formal word and, used figuratively, stresses that only a hollow shell remains.

disembowel: To disembowel is strictly literal: to remove the internal organs of a body. Eviscerate shares that grisly literal sense but has moved on — today it is mostly used figuratively, for stripping an argument, budget, or institution of its essential substance.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

reinforce: strengthen or support something

Where it sits · how much of it is stripped away

weaken → eviscerate → erase

weaken vs. eviscerate: Weakening something reduces its strength; eviscerating it removes its essential substance almost entirely.

erase vs. eviscerate: Eviscerate guts the core of something while it may still exist in form; to erase it completely wipes it out of existence.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — e-: out (Latin (ex-))

root — viscer: internal organs (Latin (viscera))

suffix — -ate: to make or perform an action (Latin)

Put it together: Eviscerate comes from Latin e- ('out') + viscera ('internal organs') + -ate -- literally 'to take the organs out.'

Use the root in a new word: visceral: Critics called the documentary's opening minutes the most visceral footage of the year.

Word Choice

Eviscerate is used both literally (removing an animal's organs) and, very commonly, in a non-literal sense for utterly destroying an argument, a budget, or a reputation.
